people/william-lane-craig/summary: American evangelical philosopher who revived the medieval Islamic kalām cosmological argument (1979), defends the historicity of Jesus’ resurrection and Molinism, and has debated leading atheists worldwide; a leading representative of classical apologetics.
people/richard-swinburne/summary: British philosopher at Oxford whose The Existence of God (1979) argues by Bayesian probability that a cumulative case from the universe’s existence, order, consciousness, morality, miracles and religious experience makes theism more probable than not. Raised Anglican, he joined the Orthodox Church in 1996.
people/theodore-abu-qurrah/summary: Melkite (Chalcedonian) bishop of Harran and one of the first Christian theologians to write in Arabic. He defended the Trinity, incarnation and the veneration of icons in dialogue with Muslim kalām theologians, and proposed criteria for discerning the true religion among many.
people/theodore-abu-qurrah/keyIdeas/1: Defence of icons in an Islamic context
people/karl-pfander/summary: German Pietist missionary (Basel Mission, later Church Missionary Society) in Persia, India and Istanbul whose Mizan al-Haqq (Balance of Truth, 1829) became the most widely circulated Christian apologetic to Muslims. He lost the public Agra debate (1854) to Rahmatullah Kairanawi.
people/caesarius-of-arles/summary: Bishop of Arles (502-542), popular preacher and monastic legislator, who presided over the Second Council of Orange (529) that settled the semi-Pelagian controversy in favour of a moderate Augustinianism.
people/david-bentley-hart/summary: American Orthodox theologian and translator of the New Testament (2017) whose That All Shall Be Saved (2019) argues that eternal torment is incompatible with God as creator ex nihilo and perfect goodness.
people/david-bentley-hart/keyIdeas/1: Classical theism and the goodness of God
people/e-p-sanders/summary: American scholar whose Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) argued that Second Temple Judaism was a religion of grace ("covenantal nomism"), not legalistic works-righteousness, launching what became the New Perspective on Paul.
people/hannah-whitall-smith/summary: American Quaker-born Holiness writer whose The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life (1875), with the Brighton and Oxford conventions she and her husband Robert Pearsall Smith led, helped launch the Keswick "higher life" movement.
people/john-cassian/summary: Monk trained among the Desert Fathers of Egypt who founded monasteries at Marseille; his Conferences (c.426-429), especially Conference 13, held that the first movement toward God can arise from the human will, assisted by grace — a view later labelled "semi-Pelagian". He is venerated as a saint in East and West.
people/john-cassian/keyIdeas/1: Desert spirituality transmitted to the West
people/john-gill/summary: English Particular Baptist pastor in Southwark and learned commentator; often associated with "high" or hyper-Calvinism for teaching eternal justification and reluctance to offer the gospel indiscriminately, though scholars debate how far he denied the free offer.
people/john-macarthur/summary: Pastor of Grace Community Church, Sun Valley, California, whose The Gospel According to Jesus (1988) argued that saving faith includes submission to Christ as Lord, sparking the "lordship salvation" debate.
people/luis-de-molina/summary: Spanish Jesuit whose Concordia (1588) reconciled grace, foreknowledge and free will through God’s "middle knowledge" (scientia media) of what free creatures would do in any circumstance; this provoked the De Auxiliis controversy with the Dominicans.
people/moise-amyraut/summary: French Huguenot theologian at the Academy of Saumur whose Brief Traitté de la prédestination (1634), developing John Cameron, taught a "hypothetical universalism": Christ died for all on condition of faith, while God elects some to receive faith.
people/moise-amyraut/keyIdeas/1: Universal conditional decree prior to particular election
people/thomas-talbott/summary: American philosopher (Willamette University) whose The Inescapable Love of God (1999) argued on biblical and philosophical grounds that God’s love will eventually win every person freely.
people/william-durham/summary: Chicago pastor baptized in the Spirit at Azusa Street (1907) who in 1910 preached "the Finished Work of Calvary": sanctification is received at conversion by identification with Christ and then progressively appropriated, rejecting a separate second work of entire sanctification.
people/zane-hodges/summary: Dallas Theological Seminary professor and co-founder of the Grace Evangelical Society (1986), leading exponent of "free grace" theology: eternal life is received by believing Jesus’ promise, without requiring commitment to his lordship or evidence of fruit.
people/zane-hodges/keyIdeas/1: Assurance from the promise, not from works
people/vincent-of-lerins/summary: Gallic monk of the island monastery of Lérins whose Commonitorium (434) proposed the canon that the catholic faith is what has been believed ‘everywhere, always, by all’, and allowed for development as organic growth.
people/john-henry-newman/summary: Leader of the Anglican Oxford Movement who became a Catholic in 1845 and a cardinal in 1879. His Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine (1845) argued that doctrine grows organically; canonised in 2019.
people/ignaz-von-dollinger/summary: Leading German Catholic church historian at Munich who opposed the definition of papal infallibility on historical grounds; excommunicated in 1871, he inspired but did not formally join the Old Catholic movement.
people/julius-wellhausen/summary: German biblical scholar whose Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1878, 1883) gave classic form to the documentary hypothesis (J, E, D, P) and to a developmental history of Israelite religion. He resigned his theology chair (1882) over the tension between his scholarship and training ministers.
people/julius-wellhausen/keyIdeas/1: Late dating of the Priestly source
people/b-b-warfield/summary: Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield, professor at Princeton Theological Seminary (1887–1921), the most influential defender of biblical inerrancy and of Old Princeton Calvinism; also a critic of Pentecostal-type claims (Counterfeit Miracles, 1918).
people/albert-outler/summary: American Methodist historian and ecumenist, observer at Vatican II, who coined the term ‘Wesleyan quadrilateral’ to describe Wesley's use of Scripture, tradition, reason and experience.
people/athenagoras/summary: Athenian Christian philosopher whose Plea for the Christians (c.177), addressed to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, rebutted charges of atheism, cannibalism and incest. It contains an early statement of the Trinity and argues that Christians, who regard abortion and infant exposure as murder, could hardly be guilty of killing.
people/john-colenso/summary: First Anglican bishop of Natal, a translator of the Bible into isiZulu and advocate for Zulu rights. His Remarks on the Proper Treatment of Cases of Polygamy (1855/1862) argued that polygamous converts should be baptised without being forced to put away their wives; his critical work on the Pentateuch (1862–79) led to his deposition by Bishop Robert Gray (1863), a cause célèbre that prompted the first Lambeth Conference (1867).
people/beverly-harrison/summary: Feminist Presbyterian ethicist whose Our Right to Choose (1983) set out a Christian moral case for legal abortion, grounding it in women’s moral agency, the social conditions of pregnancy and a critique of the church’s historical teaching.
people/guigo-ii/summary: Ninth prior of the Grande Chartreuse whose Ladder of Monks (Scala claustralium, c.1150-1180) described lectio divina as four rungs: reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation, the classic formulation of the practice.
people/johannes-tauler/summary: Strasbourg Dominican, disciple of Meister Eckhart, whose vernacular sermons taught detachment, humility and the birth of God in the "ground" of the soul in pastoral, practical form. Luther read and praised him, and the Theologia Germanica belongs to the same circle of the "Friends of God".
people/geert-groote/summary: Dutch scholar of Deventer who, after a conversion around 1374, became a penitential preacher and founded the Devotio Moderna, from which grew the Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life and the Windesheim canons.
people/thomas-a-kempis/summary: Canon of Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, trained by the Brothers of the Common Life, traditionally the author of The Imitation of Christ (c.1418-27), probably the most widely read Christian book after the Bible.
people/nicodemus-the-hagiorite/summary: Athonite monk who with Macarius of Corinth compiled the Philokalia (Venice, 1782), an anthology of hesychast texts from the 4th to the 15th century, and edited the Pedalion (canon law) and many other works. He is honoured as a saint in the Orthodox Church.
